idiom_name: async generators plus for await...of over platform streams (Response.body, node:stream, fs.createReadStream)
implementation_notes: Async iteration is part of the language, so staged acquisition is written as a loop: fetch resolves when the response headers are available and leaves Response.body as a ReadableStream whose chunks are pulled by for await...of, and the async iterator protocol calls the iterator's return() when the loop exits early, which is where the abandoned stage is cleaned up. Node carries the same shape for local resources - fs.createReadStream opens the descriptor and reads incrementally, and stream.Readable is async-iterable - while a dynamic import() defers the acquisition of a module's whole body to first use. The classic structure is still justified when many consumers share one expensive part (a bare generator re-runs per consumer and a stream can be consumed once, so it needs tee() or an explicit cache) or when stages have to be resumable across processes.
code_sketch:
const res = await fetch(url);                     // stage 1: status + headers only
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(String(res.status)); // reject before paying for the body
for await (const chunk of res.body) {             // stage 2: bytes as they arrive
  await sink.write(chunk);                        // bounded by consumer speed
}                                                 // early break runs stream cleanup
pitfalls: An unread body keeps the request (and the connection) alive: abandoning a response without consuming or cancelling res.body leaves the expensive stage occupied until a transport timeout or GC pressure cleans it up.
A ReadableStream can be consumed once: locking it with getReader() and then iterating it throws, and two consumers require tee(), which buffers the slower branch in memory.
for await...of also accepts sync iterables but awaits every value, which MDN notes is measurably slower than for...of - the async protocol only pays for itself on real async sources.
Chunk boundaries are not record boundaries, so a staged reader needs a decoder that can carry a partial token across chunks; otherwise the stage silently corrupts records.
